label: Least-squares Minimization
notes: This appendix spans printed pages 588 through 596 and supplies the linear-algebra engine behind almost every estimator in the book. We separate two problems: the inhomogeneous fit that minimizes the distance from b to a column space, and the homogeneous fit that hunts for a null direction. Both are projection statements in disguise.

label: Two Problems
notes: Frame the appendix as exactly two templates. The inhomogeneous problem has a target vector b and asks for the closest reachable prediction. The homogeneous problem has no target and asks for the unit vector that A annihilates most nearly. Almost every DLT step in the book instantiates the second template.

label: Geometric View
notes: Walk students slowly through the projection picture. The set of all predictions Ax is the column space, a flat through the origin. The closest point to b is the foot of the perpendicular, and the residual that connects them is orthogonal to every column. That orthogonality is the entire optimality certificate.

label: Normal Equations
notes: Derive the normal equations by demanding the residual be orthogonal to each column, which is A transpose times the residual equals zero. The result is a square symmetric system. Emphasize it is correct but forms A transpose A explicitly, an operation that we will see squares the conditioning of the data.

label: Conditioning
notes: This is the practical warning of the appendix. Solving the normal equations squares the condition number, so nearly dependent columns turn a stable fit into a fragile one. The notebook's log-log plot tracks observed conditioning against the square reference; tie the solution gap annotations to lost digits of accuracy.

label: QR and SVD
notes: Present QR and SVD as the stable alternatives that never form A transpose A. QR orthogonalizes the columns; SVD factors A into rotations and stretches and gives the pseudo-inverse directly. For full column rank the pseudo-inverse reproduces the normal-equation answer without squaring the condition number.

label: Homogeneous Problem
notes: Now switch templates. With no target vector, scaling x to zero would trivially win, so we constrain the norm to one. Minimizing the Rayleigh quotient over the unit sphere selects the right singular vector belonging to the smallest singular value. That vector is the best approximate null direction of A.

label: DLT Null-space
notes: Connect the homogeneous solver to the direct linear transform. Stacking point correspondences builds a measurement matrix whose exact null vector would be the true homography or fundamental matrix. With noise there is no exact null vector, so we take the smallest singular vector as the least-squares estimate, then reshape it.

label: Total Least Squares
notes: Contrast ordinary and total least squares using the line-fit panel. Ordinary least squares trusts the horizontal coordinate and measures vertical residuals; total least squares treats both image coordinates as noisy and minimizes orthogonal distance via the smallest singular vector. In image geometry the orthogonal residual is the honest one.

label: Weighted and Constrained
notes: Cover the two modeling extensions. Weights rescale rows by measurement confidence so trusted observations pull harder, giving weighted normal equations. Linear constraints are enforced with Lagrange multipliers, producing a bordered system. Both keep the projection structure intact while changing the inner product or the feasible set.

label: Sparse Systems and Recap
notes: Close on structure and synthesis. The camera-point normal matrix is sparse and symmetric because most parameters never share an observation; reading it as a bipartite graph is why bundle adjustment is tractable. Recap the checklist: is the residual orthogonal, is the system well conditioned, is the residual measured in the right space.
